title: 1. Problem statement
text:
Operating Systems | Race Conditions and Synchronization in xv6
5
1. Problem statement
An operating system allows several activities to progress concurrently. On a multicore machine,
two CPUs can execute kernel code at the same time. A shared data structure can become
inconsistent when one CPU reads or changes it while another CPU is partway through an
update. The resulting behavior can depend on timing rather than on the intended program logic.
This study asks how synchronization protects the xv6 physical-page allocator when concurrent
processes repeatedly request and release memory. The shared structure is kmem.freelist, a linked
list of available physical pages. The investigation compares the normal allocator, a deliberately
unlocked experimental variant, and the allocator after its original locking is restored.
Practical question
Under the same four-CPU workload, do the recorded outcomes change when the existing
allocator lock calls are removed and then restored? The study uses a healthy original-lock
baseline as a control, changes only the intended allocator calls for the unlocked phase, and
checks restoration before the final phase.
What is being tested
The workload runs as four xv6 user processes, but the deliberately unprotected shared data is in
the kernel. The children have separate virtual address spaces. Their memory-management
system calls converge on the same physical allocator, making kernel-level coordination
necessary even though each child expects a private buffer.
Scope and success criteria
Success means explaining the shared-data invariant, identifying the protected operations,
documenting the controlled change, preserving every attempt, and connecting observations to
the source without inventing an internal execution trace. Other synchronization methods are
explained for comparison; only the existing xv6 allocator spinlock is evaluated experimentally.
The measurements describe a specific revision, workload, and emulator configuration. They
provide evidence for these tested conditions rather than proof that every locked program is
correct or that every unlocked execution must fail.

title: 2. Introduction, objectives and motivation
text:
Operating Systems | Race Conditions and Synchronization in xv6
6
2. Introduction, objectives and motivation
A race condition occurs when correctness depends on the relative timing of concurrent activities.
A data race is a more specific case involving conflicting memory accesses that lack the required
synchronization. At least one conflicting access is a write. A race condition can also involve a
longer sequence of individually protected operations when that sequence is not coordinated as a
whole.
A shared resource is data or a device that multiple activities can access. A critical section is the
part of a program that accesses shared state whose invariant must be preserved. Mutual
exclusion permits only one participant at a time in the sections guarded by the same lock.
Atomicity means an operation is indivisible with respect to the other participating operations; a
source statement is not automatically atomic.
Table 2. Illustrative lost update: counter starts at 0
Step
Activity A
Activity B
1
Read counter as 0
2
Read counter as 0
3
Compute 0 + 1
Compute 0 + 1
4
Store 1
5
Store 1
Two increments should produce 2, but this possible schedule leaves 1. The expression
counter++ usually involves a read, a calculation, and a write. This table illustrates the idea; it is
not a safe executable C experiment with an ordinary unsynchronized shared variable, because C
data races have undefined behavior.
Objectives and motivation
The objectives are to recognize shared kernel state, explain harmful interleavings, understand
the locking mechanism, and compare recorded outcomes before removal, after removal, and
after restoration. The motivation is to connect synchronization theory to a small, inspectable
operating system and a repeatable C workload.

title: 3. Problems caused by race conditions
text:
Operating Systems | Race Conditions and Synchronization in xv6
7
3. Problems caused by race conditions
A race may produce the right output in many executions and fail only under a particular
schedule. This makes debugging difficult: additional logging, a different compiler, or a different
CPU count can change timing. A successful run therefore cannot establish that an
unsynchronized algorithm is safe.
Table 3. Consequences of unsafe concurrent access
Problem
Explanation and example
Lost update
One write overwrites another completed update, such as a missing counter
increment or a lost free-list insertion.
Inconsistent state
A reader observes only part of a multi-step update and uses a structure whose
invariant is temporarily broken.
Corruption
An unintended writer changes data that another process expects to own; the
workload checks for changed byte tags.
Resource errors
A possible allocator race can lose a free page or return a page incorrectly. The
workload does not identify every such error.
Crash or trap
A damaged structure may lead to invalid memory access. A panic alone does not
identify the precise race.
Unpredictable behavior
The timing of conflicting accesses changes the observed outcome between
executions.
Race condition versus deadlock
A race concerns incorrect interaction between concurrent operations. A deadlock concerns
participants waiting indefinitely for conditions that cannot be satisfied, such as two activities
holding different locks while each waits for the other. Locks can prevent a race but can
introduce deadlock if used incorrectly. A host timeout is an observation of missing completion
within a limit; it is not proof of deadlock.
Misleading fixes
Adding a delay or printing more output may change timing without fixing the shared-data rule.
volatile does not provide mutual exclusion or the required inter-thread ordering. Disabling
interrupts on one CPU does not stop another CPU from changing the same data. A correct
solution must coordinate every relevant access to the invariant.

title: 4. Existing xv6 system and background
text:
Operating Systems | Race Conditions and Synchronization in xv6
8
4. Existing xv6 system and background
xv6 is a small Unix-like teaching operating system. The fixed RISC-V source revision used here
already contains synchronization. Its physical allocator manages 4096-byte pages through a
global linked list. Each free page begins with a struct run containing the next pointer, and
kmem.freelist identifies the first free page.
kalloc() removes the head page. kfree() inserts a page at the head after validating and filling it
with a diagnostic pattern. Both operations acquire kmem.lock while changing the shared list.
The practical problem is deliberately introduced by removing those calls; standard xv6 is not
being described as an allocator without locks.
Table 4. Existing mechanisms and their responsibilities
Mechanism
Purpose in the examined source
kmem.lock
Serializes allocator free-list updates in kalloc() and kfree().
Atomic exchange
Makes ownership acquisition an indivisible read-modify-write operation.
Acquire/release ordering
Constrains memory ordering around the protected operations.
push_off() / pop_off()
Manage nested local interrupt disabling while spinlocks are held.
Sleep-lock
Allows a waiting process to sleep for suitable longer operations; distinct
from the allocator spinlock.
Background search and existing-system drawbacks
The local source is the authority for exact implementation details. The MIT xv6 locking chapter
provides background on locks, invariants, and contention. POSIX synchronization
documentation supplies comparison terminology for user-space primitives. The general methods
are not all implemented by this case study.
A single allocator lock is easy to reason about, but simultaneous requests contend for it and enter
the protected list updates one at a time. Busy waiting can consume CPU cycles. These are design
tradeoffs rather than measured performance findings here. Removing the lock sacrifices
correctness instead of solving contention. Designs such as per-CPU free lists require a separate
correctness argument and are future work.

title: 5. Synchronization types: mutual exclusion
text:
Operating Systems | Race Conditions and Synchronization in xv6
9
5. Synchronization types: mutual exclusion
Synchronization coordinates access to shared state or the order of events. Mutual exclusion and
condition synchronization solve related but different problems. The correct primitive depends on
the resource, expected waiting time, execution context, and whether the protected operation may
sleep.
Table 5. Methods for controlling access
Method
Typical use
Important limitation
Mutex
One owner protects a shared object;
contended blocking mutexes can put
threads to sleep.
All participants must use the same
discipline; ownership and lock order
matter.
Spinlock
A CPU repeatedly tries an atomic
operation; useful for short kernel sections
where sleeping is unsuitable.
Waiting consumes CPU time; do not sleep
while holding an ordinary xv6 spinlock.
Reader-writer lock
Several readers may enter together; a
writer needs exclusive access.
Not a free speed improvement; fairness
and starvation depend on policy.
Atomic operation
An indivisible load, store, exchange, or
read-modify-write on a supported object.
An atomic field alone does not preserve a
multi-field invariant.
Binary semaphore
A permit count of zero or one can gate
access.
Ownership semantics differ from a mutex;
signaling must match the protocol.
Why the allocator uses a spinlock
The free-list push and pop are short operations in a kernel that can run on multiple CPUs. The
lock protects the relationship between the head and the next pointer while an update is in
progress. The spinlock is an existing upstream mechanism retained or restored by this study, not
a new implementation of all synchronization types.
Atomicity is a building block
A plain check followed by a plain assignment is insufficient to claim lock ownership: two CPUs
could both observe the lock as free. Atomic exchange combines the check and change. The
critical section still needs the correct data-structure algorithm and the correct memory-ordering
rules.

title: 6. Synchronization types: event coordination
text:
Operating Systems | Race Conditions and Synchronization in xv6
10
6. Synchronization types: event coordination
Table 6. Methods for coordinating progress
Method
Purpose
Correct-use rule
Counting semaphore
Tracks available permits, such as a
bounded resource pool; waiting consumes
a permit and posting returns one.
Choose the initial count and balance
operations; it does not automatically
protect every field.
Condition variable
Waits for a predicate, such as a nonempty
queue, together with a mutex.
Check the predicate in a while loop;
waiting releases and later reacquires the
mutex.
Monitor
Groups shared state with operations under
an exclusion rule, often using condition
variables.
Maintain its invariant and use the
language or library wait protocol
correctly.
Barrier
Stops participants at a phase boundary
until the required participants arrive.
It does not provide mutual exclusion for
updates performed inside a phase.
Sleep-lock
Lets a waiting xv6 process sleep while
another process owns the resource.
Suitable contexts may sleep; use the xv6
sleep/wakeup rules and avoid
incompatible lock nesting.
Mutual exclusion and ordering are complementary
A mutex answers who may modify an object now. A condition variable answers when a
participant may proceed after a state change. A barrier answers whether all participants have
reached a phase boundary. These primitives are not interchangeable. For example, a barrier
before two increments can make their overlap more likely without making the increments safe.
A producer-consumer queue commonly uses a mutex for the queue invariant and conditions for
empty or full states. The condition wait must atomically release the mutex and begin waiting,
then reacquire the mutex before returning. The predicate is checked again because a wakeup
does not guarantee it is still true.
These examples explain selection principles. This experiment does not compare their speed or
execute separate mutex, semaphore, barrier, or reader-writer implementations. The practical
results concern the existing xv6 allocator spinlock only.

title: 7. Proposed solution and working flow
text:
Operating Systems | Race Conditions and Synchronization in xv6
11
7. Proposed solution and working flow
The solution is to retain or restore kmem.lock around every relevant free-list update. With
consistent use, one CPU completes a push or pop before another CPU begins a conflicting
update. The lock protects the list invariant, not merely the variable name. Correctness also
assumes the code inside the critical section is correct and that callers respect allocation
ownership.
acquire(&kmem.lock)
    read or modify kmem.freelist and list links
release(&kmem.lock)
Figure 1. The allocator critical section, expressed as a source-level flow.
How acquisition and release work
In the examined source, acquire() first invokes push_off() and checks whether the current CPU
already holds the lock. It repeatedly calls __atomic_exchange_n with __ATOMIC_ACQUIRE
until the old lock value is zero. It then records the owner CPU. Atomic exchange prevents two
CPUs from winning the same ownership transition.
release() checks ownership, clears the owner record, stores zero with __ATOMIC_RELEASE,
and invokes pop_off(). Acquire and release ordering keep the protected memory accesses on the
appropriate side of the ownership transition. The hardware and compiler must respect these
constraints; mutual exclusion cannot be built by treating ordinary loads and stores as an atomic
pair.
Interrupt handling and correct lock use
Nested interrupt handling records the prior interrupt state and disables local interrupts while
needed. This helps avoid same-CPU interruption and re-entry problems while holding a
spinlock. It does not replace cross-CPU locking. Removing allocator acquire/release calls also
removes their interrupt-handling effects where no outer lock is active, so the experiment does
not isolate those effects independently.
Use a consistent lock order, keep the section short, and match each acquisition with release on
every applicable path. Avoid sleeping while holding an ordinary xv6 spinlock. The working
experimental flow is original locking, controlled removal, identical workload, exact restoration,
and repeated measurement.

title: 12. Possible allocator interleavings
text:
Operating Systems | Race Conditions and Synchronization in xv6
16
12. Possible allocator interleavings
The following schedules explain possible failures at source level. They are theoretical
interleavings, not instruction traces recovered from the recorded experiments. The raw logs
show symptoms but do not identify the exact internal schedule.
Table 8. Possible double allocation without locking
Step
CPU 0
CPU 1
1
Read head page P
2
Read the same head P
3
Advance head to P.next
4
Advance head to P.next
5
Return P
Return P
Both CPUs can observe the same head before either update excludes the other. In this simplified
schedule, both return P. Correct locking makes each pop occur as a complete protected
operation, so the second CPU observes the updated list instead.
Table 9. Possible lost free page without locking
Step
CPU 0 frees X
CPU 1 frees Y
1
Set X.next to old head H
2
Set Y.next to old head H
3
Set head to X
4
Set head to Y
The final chain is Y followed by H, and the new link to X has been overwritten. X is no longer
reachable through the free-list head in this example. One lock around the complete push
prevents the two insertions from overlapping in that way.
These examples describe why list invariants need coordination. They do not establish that a
particular recorded corruption, allocation failure, or trap was caused by exactly one of these
schedules. The test can miss lost pages or damage outside the buffers it verifies.

title: 16. Restoration and verification
text:
Operating Systems | Race Conditions and Synchronization in xv6
20
16. Restoration and verification
After the unlocked phase, the exact saved original allocator is restored. The restoration check
validates its checksum, the final allocator diff is empty, and the restored kernel is rebuilt.
C01-C10 then repeat the same workload in fresh guests. This closes the experiment with the
original synchronization in place.
restoration-check.txt:
kernel/kalloc.c: OK
final-restoration.diff:
(empty file)
test-verification.txt:
user/race_test.c: OK
Figure 9. Rendered verification excerpts from the C-validation evidence folder.
xv6 kernel is booting
hart 3 starting
hart 1 starting
hart 2 starting

$ race_test
race_test: children=4 pages=8 rounds=200
race_test: PASS (all 4 children completed)
$ QEMU: Terminated
Figure 10. Rendered C-validation C01 console excerpt after allocator restoration.
All ten restored attempts reported PASS. The baseline and restored phases therefore show the
same observed completion count, while the unlocked phase shows no PASS outcomes under this
workload. The return to passing results supports the importance of the original locking
discipline in this controlled comparison.
The checksum and empty diff are evidence of restoration at the time the run set was collected.
They are not a claim that this report preparation performed a new kernel build. The preserved
final-restored-build.txt contains the recorded final build output.

The normal and restored allocator phases each produced ten PASS outcomes. All ten unlocked
attempts produced a non-PASS primary outcome. The comparison supports retaining the
original locking discipline under the tested configuration. It does not establish a universal
numerical failure probability for other workloads or computers.
How the evidence supports the explanation
Source analysis identifies free-list updates that require a coherent relationship between the head
and links. The controlled diff removes their common protection. The observed failures appear in
that phase, and observed completion returns after restoration. This provides a useful practical
connection between the invariant, its synchronization mechanism, and the recorded behavior.
Limitations
The test verifies its own byte buffers and process completion; it can miss lost pages, overwritten
corruption, or damage elsewhere. The logs are not an instruction-level trace. Failure messages
can interleave, and primary categories summarize attempts with more than one symptom.
Removing the lock calls also removes their local interrupt-management effects in some contexts.
The data covers one revision, one workload, four virtual CPUs, and ten attempts per phase.
Elapsed time includes host-side output collection, so it should not be used as a speed
comparison. An unlocked pass would not prove safety, and the absence of locked failures is
evidence limited to the tested attempts.
Demonstration material
The accompanying PPT links to demo-walkthrough.mp4. That file is an earlier-run walkthrough
rendered from saved source and logs, not a live screen recording and not a recording of this
C-validation set. Use it to explain the procedure; use Tables 12-14 and the C-validation logs for
the report results.

title: 20. Conclusion, applications and future scope
text:
Operating Systems | Race Conditions and Synchronization in xv6
24
20. Conclusion, applications and future scope
This case study connects race-condition theory with a concrete kernel data structure. Four
concurrent C workers repeatedly allocate and release memory through xv6. Standard xv6
protects the shared physical-page free list with kmem.lock. Temporarily removing its existing
calls exposes unsafe concurrent interaction; restoring them returns the tested workload to
observed completion.
In the C-validation set, original locks passed in 10 of 10 attempts, the unlocked variant passed in
0 of 10, and restored locks passed in 10 of 10. These results support the original locking
discipline for the tested conditions. They do not identify an exact failing instruction schedule or
prove the absence of all races.
What was learned
A short source operation may contain several machine-level actions. Synchronization must
protect the invariant across the whole critical section. Atomic ownership operations and memory
ordering support the lock, while nested interrupt handling addresses local execution constraints.
All relevant accesses must obey the same rule; a lock around only one caller is insufficient.
Different synchronization types serve different purposes. Mutexes and spinlocks control
ownership, condition variables coordinate predicates, semaphores manage permits, and barriers
align phases. Using a primitive with the wrong protocol can leave a race or introduce deadlock.
The comparison methods were explained conceptually; the experimental mechanism was the
allocator spinlock.
Applications
The same reasoning applies to operating-system memory lists, shared queues, caches, file
metadata, and application state such as inventory or account updates. In each case, identify the
invariant, choose a coordination rule suitable for the context, and check that all participants
follow it. Particular applications need their own implementation and validation.
Future scope
Further work could vary CPU count and workload size, add checks for lost pages, investigate
another shared kernel structure, or measure lock contention with an appropriate benchmark.
Per-CPU allocator designs could reduce contention but require careful transfer rules. These
extensions have not been performed in this case study.
